claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: Fix a plane embedding and retain the K_{2,k} subgraph H on {p,q}∪B, where k=|B|. For k≥3, H is 2-connected. It has k+2 vertices and 2k edges, so Euler's formula gives k faces. Every facial boundary is an even cycle of length at least four, while their total length is 4k; therefore every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. A connected component disjoint from H lies wholly in one face, so its B-neighbors are contained in that face's two consecutive gates. For k≤2 the bound is immediate.
claims.search_method: Direct topological proof for an arbitrary plane embedding, including the outer face and the cases |B|≤2.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Conditions (i) and (ii) give an immediate exit or a move to a gate whose two exit edges cannot both be deleted before the next move. Under (iii), after s→w the two triples {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} are edge-disjoint, so one remains intact after Nemesis's deletion; moving through that gate then leaves two exit edges against one further deletion. Conversely, if none holds, after the first move to w its outside component has at most two boundary gates and w sees at most one. Nemesis prepares a seen gate by deleting one exit edge; any other boundary gate requires an intervening move, providing a turn to prepare it too. On entry to a prepared gate, Nemesis deletes its other exit edge. Since B is independent, leaving a dead gate enters another outside component whose boundary contains that gate and at most one new gate, which can be prepared on the intervening move. This invariant prevents entry into an unprepared gate until finite edge depletion ends the game. The conditions are testable by adjacency scans. Exact minimax found no mismatch across 1,622 small graphs satisfying the same two-boundary property and 11,354 starting states.
claims.search_method: Completed gate-preparation invariant proof plus exhaustive exact minimax over decomposition-class graphs through seven vertices; this search class is broader than the planar promise.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Discarding exit-exit edges is outcome-neutral. Replace every regular-exit incidence by a uniquely labeled exit leaf. Before escape, regular moves and relevant deletions correspond edge-for-edge, and a regular position is connected to an original exit exactly when it is connected to a corresponding leaf, so the game outcome is preserved. In case (a), the transformed graph is a forest because only leaves were added to the regular forest. In case (b), each regular degree is preserved and every new exit has degree one, so the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The source's established linear-time tree and maximum-degree-three algorithms therefore apply after a linear-size transformation. Exhaustive checking of all 1,024 graphs on three regular vertices and two exits produced zero outcome mismatches across 3,072 regular starts; it also checked 896 forest and 854 degree-three transformations.
claims.search_method: Outcome-preserving reduction proof, application of the source theorem, and exhaustive exact validation of exit splitting on all small labeled instances described in the evidence.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: Integer segment tests verify the stated drawing has no vertex on a nonincident edge and no crossing among all 21 nonincident edge pairs. The strategy is sound: play s→c. If the first deletion is bc, play c→z; the two three-edge arms through a and b are disjoint, so one remains intact and supplies two exit edges against the next deletion. Otherwise play c→b. If bp or bq remains, escape immediately; if both were deleted, they were exactly the first two deletions, so b→a leaves both ap and aq intact before the next deletion. After exit splitting, the only possible roots within distance one of s are s and c. The regular degree-one vertex s cannot root a full binary tree. At c, the regular leaf s is forbidden, forcing children b and z; then z has only a and the already-used sibling b available besides parent c, so it cannot have two children in a tree. Exact enumeration rejected all 2,046 nonempty edge-subset/root candidates, and exact minimax confirms the fugitive wins.
claims.witness: Vertices p,q,s,a,b,c,z with edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs and integer coordinates a=(0,0), b=(120,0), p=(60,80), q=(60,-80), z=(60,40), c=(90,10), s=(80,23).
claims.search_method: Exact integer straight-line planarity test, exact alternating-game minimax, explicit strategy audit, and exhaustive full-binary-exit-tree enumeration after exit splitting.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: With the existential move scoped outside the disjunction, the recurrence exactly matches the move-then-delete rules: reaching an exit wins before deletion, while every possible Nemesis deletion must otherwise preserve exit connectivity and a winning successor state. Each recursive call adds one edge to D, so recursion depth is at most m. There are at most n·2^m states and only polynomial work per transition; memoization gives O*(2^m) time, while depth-first evaluation uses polynomial space. For a simple planar graph with n≥3, m≤3n−6, yielding O*(8^n). A separately coded explicit Fugitive-turn/Nemesis-turn evaluator agreed with the recurrence on all 5,120 deleted-set/current-regular-vertex states of the seven-vertex witness.
claims.search_method: Direct quantifier and state-space proof, with exhaustive comparison against an independently structured alternating-turn evaluator.

target_evidence: The exact target requests a classification for every planar simple graph with exactly two exits, either by a polynomial-time algorithm or by a matching hardness result. The draft explicitly states that it obtains neither. Its verified structural decomposition, complete classification of one promised subclass, two additional linear-time subclasses, counterexample to a tempting certificate characterization, and exact exponential/PSPACE upper bounds are material but incomplete progress. The final writeup confines its completeness assertion to the verified same-independent-neighborhood subclass and accurately labels the overall resolution PARTIAL; it neither overstates nor understates target coverage.
